summary: Defines serial number arithmetic, the rules for comparing and incrementing the wrapping counters that DNS uses. The idea was widely understood but never formally written down. It updates RFC 1034 and RFC 1035.

plainLanguage.summary: When a counter wraps around to zero, which number is newer? This explains how to compare numbers on a clock-like loop.

questions: what is dns serial number arithmetic
how to compare soa serial numbers
how to compare dns soa serial numbers
what happens when a serial number wraps
subtitle: How to compare and increment wrapping counters, such as the DNS SOA serial number, when the numbers loop back to zero.

tldr.problem: RFC 1034 and RFC 1035 said DNS serial numbers should be compared using sequence space arithmetic, a term neither defines and which the earlier IEN-74 arithmetic did not fully cover.
tldr.mechanism: It defines a serial number space of a chosen size (SERIAL_BITS) with two operations: adding a bounded positive integer modulo the space size, and comparing with a half-space rule. Some pairs of values are deliberately left unordered.
tldr.outcome: The DNS SOA serial number is a 32-bit serial number under these rules. The RFC updates RFC 1034 and RFC 1035 to refer to this arithmetic.

today: RFC 1982 is a Proposed Standard. It updates RFC 1034 and RFC 1035, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Missing Definition
sections.content:
The serial number field of the DNS SOA resource record is defined in RFC 1035 as an unsigned 32 bit version number that wraps and should be compared using sequence space arithmetic. RFC 1034 uses the same wording for secondary server consistency checks.

The problem is that neither RFC defines that term. It seems to refer to the arithmetic used for TCP sequence numbers (RFC 793), defined in IEN-74, but that arithmetic defines no general comparison operator. This RFC defines the field and its operations to clarify the original intent, and is believed to agree with current implementations.

It also notes that some older, superseded implementations treated the serial as a plain unsigned integer and ignored wrapping.
sections.plainLanguage: The old rule said to compare numbers 'the clock way' but never explained how. This RFC finally writes the clock rule down.

sections.title: The Serial Number Space
sections.content:
Serial numbers are non-negative integers from a finite range. The lowest is zero, and the maximum is always one less than a power of two. Seen as serial numbers, no value is special: there is no minimum or maximum, and every value has a successor and a predecessor.

To define a serial number type you give its size, called SERIAL_BITS. That is the power of two that gives one more than the largest value, and the number of bits needed to hold every value.
sections.plainLanguage: A serial number space is a circle of numbers. You only have to say how many numbers fit around it.

sections.title: Addition
sections.content:
Only two operations exist: adding a positive integer of limited range, and comparison. A serial number s may be incremented by an integer n in the range 0 to 2^(SERIAL_BITS - 1) - 1. The result is (s + n) modulo (2 ^ SERIAL_BITS), so values wrap past the top back to zero.

Adding a value outside that range is undefined.
sections.plainLanguage: You can walk forward around the circle, but only less than halfway at a time. If you pass the top number, you land back near zero.

sections.title: Comparison and Its Undefined Cases
sections.content:
Take i1 and i2 as the ordinary integers with the same numeric values as s1 and s2. They are equal only if i1 equals i2. Otherwise s1 is less than s2 if i1 < i2 and the gap i2 - i1 is below 2^(SERIAL_BITS - 1), or if i1 > i2 and the gap i1 - i2 is above that half-space value. Greater than is the mirror image.

Some unequal pairs are neither less nor greater. Using the ordering operators on them gives an undefined result. The RFC explains that a simple definition for those pairs could make s1 < s2 and s2 < s1 both true depending on test order. A fully defined test would be burdensome and still allow non-intuitive cases. Implementations may return either result or flag an error, and users should avoid letting those pairs coexist.

The corollaries follow: adding n greater than zero always gives a larger value, but after two additions whose sum is out of range, whether the result is greater or less than the start is undefined, though it is known not to be equal.
sections.plainLanguage: Whoever is less than halfway around the circle ahead of you counts as ahead. If two numbers sit exactly opposite each other, nobody is ahead, and the rule refuses to pick.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
With SERIAL_BITS of 2 the values are 0 to 3 and the largest meaningful increment is 1. Then 3+1 is 0, and 0 > 3. It is undefined whether 2 > 0 or 0 > 2.

With SERIAL_BITS of 8 the values are 0 to 255 and the largest increment is 127. Here 255+1 is 0, 100+100 is 200, and 200+100 is 44. Also 100+100 > 100, yet (100+100)+100 < 100, so incrementing can make a serial number appear smaller. The pairs 0 and 128, 1 and 129, up to 127 and 255 are unequal but unordered.
sections.plainLanguage: On a tiny clock with four numbers, going past 3 takes you back to 0. Opposite numbers cannot be ranked.

sections.title: The DNS SOA Serial Number
sections.content:
The SOA serial number is a Serial Number with SERIAL_BITS of 32, so a 32 bit unsigned integer from 0 to 4294967295. The maximum defined increment is 2147483647.

Care should be taken not to increase the serial, in one or more steps, by more than this maximum within the period given by SOA.expire. Otherwise some secondary servers may keep an out of date copy of the zone while holding a serial number that looks greater than the primary's. If the serial must be set lower, take special care to verify that all servers followed each change.

Caution is also advised before setting the serial to zero. Zero is not special in this arithmetic, but many DNS implementations have wrongly treated it as a special case.
sections.plainLanguage: The DNS version counter must not jump more than halfway around the circle before copies catch up, or old copies might look newer than the real one.
